claims.text: The coating is a single-crystal Fe33Ni32Cr11Co11Cu13 high-entropy alloy on a single-crystal Cu matrix.
The initial FeNiCrCoCu coating is fully FCC and contains no pre-existing amorphous regions.
The initial coating has high stacking-fault energy.
Nanoindentation is performed to 30 Å at 10 m/s at 300, 600, 900, and 1200 K, followed by sliding-wear simulation.
Above 900 K, the coating undergoes a sequential transition from dislocation starvation to rapid amorphization.
Thermal energy above 900 K overcomes a stacking-fault-related energy barrier and causes the FCC lattice to collapse into an HCP-like or amorphous state.
The structural evolution proceeds from FCC stacking faults through HCP-like local ordering to amorphization.
At temperatures above 900 K, thermal activation lowers the barrier for Shockley partial-dislocation dissociation and stacking-fault annihilation.
Shockley partial-dislocation activity and stacking-fault annihilation lead to dislocation starvation.
Severe lattice distortion and high entropy facilitate a thermally driven transformation to an amorphous or HCP-rich state.
Loss of crystalline order eliminates dislocation-mediated strain hardening and causes a sharp hardness decrease.
The friction-coefficient spike is caused by increased adhesive contact area and material transfer after crystalline order is lost.
The friction coefficient remains stable at 300–600 K and spikes at 900 and 1200 K.
The wear rate increases exponentially above 900 K.
The HCP fraction peaks at 900 K before total FCC-order loss and amorphization at 1200 K.
Total dislocation-line length decreases significantly at 900 K and vanishes upon amorphization.
At 300 and 600 K, dislocation density is maintained or increases slightly, producing stable hardness and low friction.
A 2.0 nm nanocrystalline CoCrFeNiMn alloy exhibits amorphization and substantial loss of FCC structure.
The single-crystal structure of FeNiCrCoCu may delay amorphization relative to 2.0 nm nanocrystalline CoCrFeNiMn.
Artificially increasing stacking-fault energy should suppress HCP formation and, if the proposed pathway is correct, suppress the friction spike.

contradictions.description: The mediator specifies progression from stacking faults to an HCP-rich intermediate, whereas the mechanism emphasizes stacking-fault annihilation as the route to starvation while concurrently predicting an HCP-rich state. The temporal relationship between fault annihilation and the proposed HCP peak is not resolved.

The hypothesis describes thermal energy as overcoming a stacking-fault-energy barrier to lattice collapse, while the mechanism separately invokes a reduced barrier for Shockley partial dissociation and stacking-fault annihilation. These are distinct processes and are treated as one causal step without explaining how dissociation, which can create stacking faults, produces their annihilation.
